newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals head further south.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals head further south.

text.p: * Regional currencies continue to weaken as speculators and investors bail out in favour of the U.S. dollar.
* Singapore dollar hits new 30-month low of 1.4610 to U.S. dollar in line with Malaysian ringgit's slide to three-year low of 2.60.
* Indonesian rupiah remains weak on ample liquidity and spillover effect from other regionals.
* Thai baht hit by strong commercial demand for dollar ahead of long weekend in Thailand.
* Philippine peso weakens in early trade.
Southeast Asian currencies headed further south on Friday as speculative funds and investors continued to bail out in favour of the U.S. dollar.

The Singapore dollar plumbed depths not seen since December 1994, falling through the psychological level of 1.46 against its U.S. counterpart as the Malaysian ringgit fell to a three-year low of 2.60.
The ringgit has come under intense pressure this week, partly due to a perceived change in stance by Malaysian authorities towards allowing market forces to determine the exchange rate.

Dealers said the Singapore dollar was weakening in line with the region's currencies, which remain vulnerable to further speculative attack and fund outflows after the de facto devaluations of the Thai baht and Philippine peso.

"Basically, it's a sympathy move against all the other regionals. Investors are pulling out of this region and moving back into the U.S. and continental Europe," said a senior trader at a Singapore-based bank.
He said Friday's moves in both the Singapore dollar and ringgit were exaggerated by thin turnover and wide spreads.

Dealers said there had been no sign in the market of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de facto central bank, but Malaysia's central Bank Negara was rumoured to have been checking rates around the 2.60 level.
"The MAS will look at it in terms of percentages with the neighbours," the dealer said, referring to its policy of monitoring the Singapore dollar against a trade weighted basket of currencies.
"They would be uncomfortable if all the neighbours weakened and the Sing dollar did not move," he said.
The Singapore dollar was quoted at 1.4605/15 to the U.S. dollar at 0420 GMT against an early high of 1.4550/60. The ringgit was at 2.5970/6000.
Dealers said the Singapore dollar was likely to head for the 1.47 level in the near term and could then slide to 1.50.
But a European bank dealer said the U.S. dollar needed to undergo a correction before heading higher.
"I'm very reluctant to buy (the U.S. dollar) at this level. When the market has turned long, they'll realise it's too high and start selling," she said.
In Indonesia, the rupiah remained weak in nervous trade as players kept a wary eye on volatility in the region.
"The market is still looking for some kind of equilibrium. "There is no clear trend yet. The feeling is that people dare not go short on dollars at present," a local bank dealer in Jakarta said.
He said operators appeared to stay squared or slightly long on dollars due to ample rupiah in the money market.
A U.S. bank dealer said spot rates were expected to range between 2,470 and 2,480 on Friday. Spot rupiah was quoted at 2,477.0/82.0 at 0420 GMT against an opening of 2,472/75.
Some dealers said Indonesia's sound fundamentals did not justify the currency attack.
The Thai baht succumbed to strong commercial demand for the dollar ahead of a long weekend in Thailand.
"The dollar was traded slightly higher (against the baht), but there wasn't any panic trading. It's just the normal situation for Friday," said one dealer at a local bank.
A Singapore-based dealer said dollar/baht was likely to move up slowly towards the 30.50 level, with buying interest expected below 30.00.
The Philippine peso remained relatively weak after opening at 28.50 against a previous close at 28.00.
Manila dealers said trading conditions were light but the dollar looked offered after its sudden drop on Thursday.
-- Syed Azman in Kuala Lumpur (603-206 2323), Mantik
